answer.rationale: The binding constraints are continuity (contract lapses in 14 days, no auto-renew, line at 94% with zero buffer) and an 18% cost mandate. Any action that does not secure primary supply is off the table, which rules out add_second_source and defer_decision as the single decision this cycle: memory_c5's deferral worked only because that renewal was explicitly non-critical and continued month-to-month, neither of which holds here. Switching primary on memory_c2 is the tempting move because it is the only memory that names a sharp unit-cost cut, but c2 is exactly the memory I most distrust: it praises onboarding speed and invoicing accuracy and is silent on defect rates, on-time delivery, and behavior under strain. Cost and invoicing are the easiest things to observe early and the last things to fail; silence on delivery performance in a record written shortly after onboarding is weak evidence of low risk, not evidence of low risk. Executing a primary migration in 14 days against a line with no buffer converts a cost problem into a stoppage. So I verify c2 to see whether the archived record actually contains delivery data or whether the consolidation dropped it. Second, memory_c6 is the strongest unexploited lever: the incumbent refused to reopen price this cycle, but c6 records that a multi-year term unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope. That is a different negotiating axis than the one already refused, and memory_c4 confirms the incumbent moves when benchmarked. Combining them gives a path to material cost reduction with zero migration risk. I verify c6 to confirm the discount magnitude and whether it plausibly approaches 18%, and to check what was conceded for it. Intended action is therefore negotiate_terms: secure continuity while trading term length and benchmark pressure for price, at standard scope rather than a sweeping commitment. Explicit risk to flag downstream: a multi-year lock-in buys this year's savings by spending future flexibility, and it entrenches single-sourcing that memory_c3 shows was the real failure mode during shortage. So any term I sign should preserve the right to qualify a second source, and add_second_source should be first in queue at next review regardless of how this negotiation lands. If verification shows c6's discount falls well short of 18% and c2's record does contain real delivery evidence, switching becomes live, but I will not treat c2's cost claim as decision-grade until its silence on delivery is resolved.
